A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MedCheck and provide readable text, figures, tables, and appendices. V1's appendices A–C can be matched to the retained and expanded material in v2's appendices A–J, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original scoring of 53 benchmarks against 46 criteria, with aggregate statistics, distributions, and benchmark-level findings.

after.justification: V2 reports an expanded 56-benchmark audit, annotator agreement, domain-specific rescoring, and original safety and clinical-transfer analyses.

M1.justification: The five-phase, 46-criterion framework and 0–2 scale remain. V2 adds a domain-specific scoring variant that selects criteria according to medical versus clinical purpose (Appendices G–H), and refines contamination scoring to recognize feasible prevention or detection measures.

E1.justification: The audit adds DR.BENCH, LCD, and MIMIC-IV-ED, extending coverage of diagnostic reasoning, long-document mortality prediction, and emergency-department prediction. Beyond documentation auditing, v2 introduces clinical-safety evaluation and a JAMA Clinical Challenge holdout involving 100 cases across 10 specialties.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates an alternative benchmark-assessment framework against MedCheck. The LLMs in v2's Tables 7–8 serve as measurement subjects for validation analyses, rather than competing assessment methods.

E3.justification: V1 describes independent expert scoring; v2 reports LLM pre-scoring followed by human verification, allocation of benchmarks among annotators, and consensus review. New validation protocols compare benchmark performance across three models against MedSafetyBench or the JAMA holdout, including a safety-focused aggregation of Phases I, III, and IV.

E4.justification: V2 adds safety-alignment and clinical-transfer validation studies (F.11–F.12), domain-specific rescoring (G), a complete worked scoring case (I), and a diagnostic recommendation example (J). These extend v1's descriptive phase-by-phase analyses with new validation questions and case studies.

E5.justification: V2 first reports inter-annotator reliability: Fleiss' kappa of 0.78 from five shared benchmarks independently scored by three annotators. It also introduces Pearson/Spearman correlations and p-values. V1's statistics principally describe the audited benchmarks and do not provide these reliability or inferential estimates.

E6.justification: Audit statistics change with the expanded corpus; for example, Appendix B.7/F.7 reports Phase III averages of 52.4% versus 52.1%. Tables 7–8 and Figures 36–37 add model, correlation, and domain-specific results. Table 8 newly reports JAMA scores of 0.750, 0.730, and 0.570 for GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Qwen2.5, respectively.

T1.justification: The disease-and-department coverage definition in Equation 1 is retained. V2's conceptual validation arguments and correlation analyses introduce no new mathematical propositions, proofs, or substantive derivations.

C1.justification: V2 narrows introductory criticism toward many newer, rapidly developed benchmarks for general-purpose LLMs and expands the stated audit from 53 to 56 benchmarks. The central contributions—the lifecycle framework, 46 criteria, and findings concerning clinical relevance, data integrity, and safety—remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive arguments about purpose-appropriate assessment, the value of dataset reuse, feasible contamination safeguards, and compatibility between privacy and openness. It introduces interpretations linking MedCheck scores to safety and clinical transfer, acknowledges the safety study's three-benchmark limitation, and specifies future limitations concerning multimodal and autonomous agents.

D1.justification: New Appendices B–C document search databases, dates, screening counts and eligibility rules, annotator calibration, evidence requirements, and adjudication procedures. They identify GPT-4o-Search-Preview, temperature 0, prompt inputs, search assistance, and JSON scoring output. Appendix I adds item-level scoring explanations absent from v1.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A substantially expand clinical-informatics positioning through TRIPOD-LLM, Med-HELM, BigBIO, MIMIC-IV, and related critiques. V2 distinguishes benchmark assessment from study reporting and model evaluation, while removing the Royce and Yas software-lifecycle references.

P1.justification: The introduction, study-design narrative, discussion, and conclusion undergo substantial paragraph rewriting. Appendix organization is extensively expanded: the original benchmark list, quantitative results, and rubrics move from A/B/C to E/F/H among new dedicated sections. Author ordering and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: V2 adds scoring and validation Tables 6–8 and domain-specific Figures 36–37. Existing plots are relocated or revised, including axis ranges and benchmark membership in phase-ranking charts, and checklist numbers gain hyperlinks. Most graphical styles and the two-column layout remain.

improvement.justification: V2 improves auditability through detailed selection and scoring protocols, agreement reporting, and purpose-sensitive analyses, and corrects some explanations and numerical summaries. However, it introduces reporting inconsistencies: v1 gives 47% safety/fairness omission in both Section 4.1 and Figure 16, whereas v2 gives 45% and 50%. The new clinical-transfer discussion also overinterprets a three-benchmark correlation with p = 0.144. These competing effects on transparency and evidential reliability prevent a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
